topics.name: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
topics.summary: Pressure is force per unit area, \( P=\dfrac{F}{A} \), measured in pascal; it is a scalar, and at a point in a fluid at rest it is the same in every direction. Below the free surface of a liquid open to the atmosphere the absolute pressure at depth \( h \) is \( P=P_{atm}+h\rho g \); the extra term \( h\rho g \) alone is the gauge pressure, measured relative to the atmosphere. Hydrostatic pressure depends only on depth and density, never on the shape, width or volume of the container (the hydrostatic paradox), so points at the same horizontal level in a connected liquid at rest are at the same pressure. Pascal's law says a pressure change applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished everywhere, which is the basis of hydraulic lifts and brakes: equal pressure on two pistons gives force proportional to area while the volumes swept are equal. Barometers measure atmospheric pressure as the height of a liquid column (76 cmHg), and open manometers read gauge pressure as a level difference. In accelerating frames replace \( g \) by the effective gravity.
topics.worked_example:
Find the absolute pressure 4 m below the surface of water (density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\)) with \( P_{atm}=1.0\times10^{5} \) Pa and \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\).

Gauge pressure \( =h\rho g=4\times1000\times10=4\times10^{4} \) Pa.

Absolute pressure \( =1.0\times10^{5}+4\times10^{4}=1.4\times10^{5} \) Pa. Reporting \( 4\times10^{4} \) Pa would be the gauge value, not the absolute one.
common_mistakes: Reporting gauge pressure when absolute pressure is asked (forgetting to add \( P_{atm} \)), or adding \( P_{atm} \) to a reading that is already absolute
Assuming a wider or fuller vessel gives a larger pressure at the same depth; only depth and density matter
In a hydraulic lift, transmitting the force instead of the pressure, or inverting the area ratio
Forgetting to convert centimetres to metres before using \( h\rho g \)
Treating pressure as a vector with a downward direction

topics.name: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
topics.summary: Archimedes' principle: a body wholly or partly immersed in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces, \( F_B=\rho_{fluid}V_{displaced}g \). The force arises from the greater hydrostatic pressure on the lower surface than on the upper surface, and it acts through the centre of buoyancy, the centre of gravity of the displaced fluid. It depends on the fluid's density and the displaced volume, not on the body's own density or mass, and (for an incompressible fluid) not on depth. For a fully submerged body \( V_{displaced} \) equals the body's volume; apparent weight is true weight minus \( F_B \), and the loss of weight in water gives the body's volume. A body floats if its density is less than the fluid's: it sinks only until the displaced fluid weighs as much as itself, so the fraction submerged is \( \dfrac{\rho_{object}}{\rho_{fluid}} \), which must lie between 0 and 1. Classic puzzles (stone thrown from a boat, ice with a nail melting, finger dipped in a beaker on a scale) are all settled by asking how much fluid is displaced before and after.
topics.worked_example:
A block of density \( 600 \) kg/m\(^3\) and volume \( 0.02 \) m\(^3\) floats in water (\( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\)), \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\). Find the buoyant force.

The block floats, so the buoyant force equals its weight: \( 600\times0.02\times10=120 \) N.

Check by displacement: fraction submerged \( =\dfrac{600}{1000}=0.6 \), so \( V_{displaced}=0.012 \) m\(^3\) and \( F_B=1000\times0.012\times10=120 \) N. Using the full \( 0.02 \) m\(^3\) would wrongly give 200 N.
common_mistakes: Using the body's own density or its full volume in \( F_B \) for a floating (partly submerged) body
Adding the buoyant force to the weight instead of subtracting it to get apparent weight
Thinking buoyancy grows with depth in an incompressible liquid
Inverting the density ratio, giving a submerged fraction greater than 1
Believing a floating body needs buoyancy greater than its weight

topics.name: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
topics.summary: In steady (streamline or laminar) flow the velocity at each point is constant in time, and streamlines never cross; flow becomes turbulent at high speed, classified by the Reynolds number \( Re=\dfrac{\rho vd}{\eta} \) (laminar below about 1000, turbulent above about 2000). For an incompressible fluid, conservation of mass gives the equation of continuity, \( A_1v_1=A_2v_2 \): where a tube narrows the fluid speeds up, and this relation involves only area and speed. Conservation of energy along a streamline of an ideal (non-viscous) fluid gives Bernoulli's equation, \( P+\tfrac12\rho v^2+\rho gh=\text{constant} \), each term being an energy per unit volume. Use continuity first to find speeds, then Bernoulli to find pressures. In a horizontal pipe the narrow section has higher speed and lower pressure, which explains the venturi meter, aerofoil lift, the Magnus effect on spinning balls, boats drawing together, and atomisers. Torricelli's law, \( v=\sqrt{2gh} \), follows from Bernoulli for efflux from a tank. Viscous fluids like honey violate Bernoulli's assumptions.
key_formulas: Range of jet from a tank: \( R=2\sqrt{h(H-h)} \)
topics.worked_example:
Water (\( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\)) flows at 1 m/s through a horizontal pipe of area \( 8 \) cm\(^2\) that narrows to \( 2 \) cm\(^2\). Find the speed in, and the pressure drop to, the narrow part.

Continuity: \( v_2=\dfrac{8\times1}{2}=4 \) m/s (no pressure needed for this step).

Bernoulli (no height change): \( P_1-P_2=\tfrac12\times1000\times(16-1)=7500 \) Pa. The pressure is lower in the narrow section, not higher.
common_mistakes: Using Bernoulli's equation to find a speed ratio, or continuity to find a pressure difference; continuity handles area-speed and Bernoulli handles pressure-speed-height
Guessing that pressure rises where a pipe narrows; it falls because the speed rises
Using the square of the speed difference instead of the difference of the squares
Using the diameter ratio instead of the area ratio in continuity
Forgetting to take the square root in Torricelli's law

topics.name: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
topics.summary: Viscosity is internal friction between adjacent fluid layers moving at different speeds. Newton's law of viscosity gives the tangential force \( F=\eta A\dfrac{dv}{dx} \), where \( \eta \) is the coefficient of viscosity (SI unit Pa s, dimensions \( [ML^{-1}T^{-1}] \)); liquid viscosity falls with temperature while gas viscosity rises. A small sphere moving slowly through a fluid feels the Stokes drag \( F=6\pi\eta rv \), valid for laminar flow at small Reynolds number. A sphere released in a fluid accelerates with decreasing acceleration as the drag builds, until drag balances weight minus buoyancy and it moves at terminal velocity \( v_t=\dfrac{2r^2(\rho_{body}-\rho_{fluid})g}{9\eta} \); the density difference (from Archimedes' principle) and the coefficient two-ninths are essential, and \( v_t\propto r^2 \), so large raindrops fall faster and coalesced drops speed up. For steady laminar flow through a tube, Poiseuille's equation gives \( Q=\dfrac{\pi\Delta Pr^4}{8\eta l} \): flow varies as the fourth power of the radius, linearly with pressure difference, and inversely with length and viscosity, and a pressure drop along a uniform tube is required to overcome viscous dissipation.
key_formulas: Coalescence of \( n \) drops: \( R=n^{1/3}r \), \( v_t\propto r^2 \)
topics.worked_example:
A sphere of radius 2 mm and density \( 2500 \) kg/m\(^3\) falls through a liquid of density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\) and viscosity \( 0.8 \) Pa s; \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\). Find the terminal velocity.

\( r^2=4\times10^{-6} \) m\(^2\), density difference \( =1500 \) kg/m\(^3\).

\( v_t=\dfrac{2\times4\times10^{-6}\times1500\times10}{9\times0.8}=\dfrac{0.12}{7.2}=\dfrac{1}{60} \) m/s. Using 2500 instead of 1500 would overestimate the speed.
common_mistakes: Using the body's density alone in the terminal-velocity formula instead of the difference with the fluid density
Using a coefficient other than two-ninths, or \( r \) instead of \( r^2 \)
Forgetting that Poiseuille flow goes as \( r^4 \), not \( r^2 \)
Thinking drag is zero at constant velocity; it is the net force that is zero
Believing liquid viscosity increases with temperature

topics.name: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
topics.summary: Surface tension \( T \) arises from cohesive forces: surface molecules have extra energy, so a liquid surface behaves like a stretched membrane and tends to minimise its area, making free drops spherical. \( T \) is the force per unit length along a line in the surface (unit N/m) and equally the surface energy per unit area (J/m\(^2\)); the work to create area \( \Delta A \) is \( T\Delta A \), so a soap film or bubble with two surfaces needs twice the area counted. \( T \) decreases with temperature and with added detergent. A curved surface sustains an excess pressure on its concave side: \( \dfrac{2T}{r} \) for a liquid drop or an air bubble inside a liquid (one surface) and \( \dfrac{4T}{r} \) for a soap bubble in air (two surfaces); smaller bubbles have higher pressure. The angle of contact \( \theta \) between liquid and solid decides wetting: acute (water on glass) gives a concave meniscus and capillary rise, obtuse (mercury on glass) gives a convex meniscus and depression. The rise is \( h=\dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{\rho gr} \), inversely proportional to the radius and to the effective gravity.
key_formulas: Drop or bubble in liquid: \( P_{excess}=\dfrac{2T}{r} \)
Work to blow a soap bubble: \( 8\pi R^2T \)
Force on a wire in a film: \( F=2Tl \)
topics.worked_example:
Compare the excess pressure in a water drop of radius 0.5 mm (\( T=0.07 \) N/m) with that in a soap bubble of the same radius (\( T=0.03 \) N/m).

Drop (one surface): \( \dfrac{2T}{r}=\dfrac{2\times0.07}{5\times10^{-4}}=280 \) Pa.

Soap bubble (two surfaces): \( \dfrac{4T}{r}=\dfrac{4\times0.03}{5\times10^{-4}}=240 \) Pa. Using \( 2T/r \) for the bubble would give 120 Pa, half the true value.
common_mistakes: Using \( 4T/r \) for a drop or an air bubble in liquid, or \( 2T/r \) for a soap bubble in air
Counting only one surface when computing the energy of a soap film or bubble
Forgetting \( \cos\theta \), or using the diameter instead of the radius, in the capillary-rise formula
Expecting liquid to overflow from a capillary tube that is too short
Confusing surface tension (N/m) with pressure (N/m\(^2\)) or viscosity (Pa s)

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: A lake is open to the atmosphere. Taking atmospheric pressure \( P_{atm}=1.0\times10^{5} \) Pa, water density \( \rho=1000 \) kg/m\(^3\) and \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the absolute pressure at a depth of 10 m is
questions.explanation:
Absolute pressure at depth \( h \) is \( P=P_{atm}+h\rho g \).

The hydrostatic (gauge) term is \( h\rho g=10\times1000\times10=1.0\times10^{5} \) Pa.

Adding atmospheric pressure: \( P=1.0\times10^{5}+1.0\times10^{5}=2.0\times10^{5} \) Pa.
questions.hint: Absolute pressure includes the atmosphere pressing on the free surface; gauge pressure is only the extra \( h\rho g \).
distractor_logic: Reports only the gauge pressure \( h\rho g \), forgetting to add atmospheric pressure for an absolute reading
Adds atmospheric pressure twice, once to the gauge term and again to an already-absolute value
Uses a depth of 1 m instead of 10 m in the hydrostatic term

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: Two vessels, one wide and one narrow, are filled with the same liquid to the same height. How do the pressures at the bottom of the two vessels compare?
options: The wider vessel has the greater bottom pressure
The narrower vessel has the greater bottom pressure
It depends on the total volume of liquid in each vessel
questions.explanation:
Hydrostatic pressure at depth \( h \) is \( P=P_{atm}+h\rho g \), which contains only the depth and the liquid density.

The shape, width or cross-sectional area of the vessel does not appear in this expression.

Since both vessels hold the same liquid to the same height, the bottom pressures are equal. This is the hydrostatic paradox.
questions.hint: Look at the formula \( P=P_{atm}+h\rho g \): does the vessel's width appear anywhere in it?
distractor_logic: Assumes more liquid overhead means more pressure, but hydrostatic pressure depends only on depth and density, not on the width of the vessel
Assumes the liquid is 'squeezed' in a narrow tube, but pressure at a given depth is independent of cross-section
Confuses total weight of liquid with pressure; pressure at a depth is set by depth and density alone

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: Pascal's law states that pressure applied to an enclosed incompressible fluid is
options: transmitted only in the downward direction due to gravity
reduced in proportion to the distance from the point of application
transmitted undiminished to every point of the fluid and to the walls of the container
concentrated at the point of application and does not spread
questions.explanation:
Pascal's law: a change in pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and to the walls of the vessel.

This is why a small force on a small piston can produce a large force on a large piston in a hydraulic press.
questions.hint: Think of a hydraulic press: the pressure produced by the small piston reaches the large piston without any loss.
distractor_logic: Confuses transmitted pressure with the weight of the fluid; applied pressure is transmitted equally in all directions
Assumes pressure 'fades' with distance, but in an enclosed fluid the applied pressure change is the same everywhere
Treats the fluid like a solid taking a point load; a fluid distributes an applied pressure throughout

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: In a hydraulic lift the smaller piston has area 10 cm\(^2\) and the larger piston has area 1000 cm\(^2\). A force of 50 N is applied on the smaller piston. The force exerted on the larger piston is
questions.explanation:
By Pascal's law the pressure is the same on both pistons: \( \dfrac{F_1}{A_1}=\dfrac{F_2}{A_2} \).

So \( F_2=F_1\dfrac{A_2}{A_1}=50\times\dfrac{1000}{10}=5000 \) N.
questions.hint: Equal pressure on both pistons means force scales with area.
distractor_logic: Inverts the area ratio, dividing by 100 instead of multiplying
Assumes the force is transmitted unchanged; it is the pressure, not the force, that is the same on both pistons
Uses an area ratio of 10 instead of the correct 100

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: One pascal (1 Pa) is equal to
questions.explanation:
Pressure is force per unit area, \( P=\dfrac{F}{A} \).

In SI units, force is in newton and area in square metre, so 1 Pa = 1 N/m\(^2\).
questions.hint: Pressure = force divided by area.
distractor_logic: Gives the unit of torque or work (newton-metre), not pressure
Gives the unit of surface tension (force per length), not force per area
Not a unit of force per area at all; kg/m has no direct physical meaning here

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: A mercury barometer reads 76 cm. If water (density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\)) were used instead of mercury (density \( 13600 \) kg/m\(^3\)), the height of the water column supported by the same atmospheric pressure would be
questions.explanation:
Atmospheric pressure equals \( h\rho g \) for the barometer liquid, so \( h_{water}\rho_{water}=h_{Hg}\rho_{Hg} \).

\( h_{water}=76\times\dfrac{13600}{1000}=76\times13.6=1033.6 \) cm.

That is 10.336 m, which is why water barometers are impractical.
questions.hint: A lighter liquid needs a taller column to produce the same pressure.
distractor_logic: Assumes the column height is independent of the liquid; the same pressure needs a taller column of a lighter liquid
Divides 76 cm by 13.6 instead of multiplying, giving a shorter water column than mercury
Rough guess that ignores the actual density ratio of 13.6

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: Take mercury density \( 13600 \) kg/m\(^3\) and \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\). The gauge pressure at a depth of 50 cm below the free surface of mercury is
questions.explanation:
Gauge pressure is only the hydrostatic term: \( P_{gauge}=h\rho g \).

\( P_{gauge}=0.5\times13600\times10=68000 \) Pa \( =6.8\times10^{4} \) Pa.

Atmospheric pressure is not added because gauge pressure is measured relative to the atmosphere.
questions.hint: Gauge pressure excludes the atmosphere; convert 50 cm to metres first.
distractor_logic: Uses the density of water instead of mercury
Uses 5 m instead of 0.5 m for the depth
Adds atmospheric pressure, giving absolute pressure when gauge pressure was asked

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: At a point inside a liquid at rest, the pressure
options: is greatest in the horizontal direction
acts only on the walls of the container, not inside the liquid
is the same in all directions
questions.explanation:
A fluid at rest cannot sustain shear stress, so the force on any small surface inside it is normal to that surface.

Considering equilibrium of a tiny element shows the pressure at a point is the same whichever way the surface is oriented.

Pressure is therefore a scalar quantity with no direction of its own.
questions.hint: Pressure is a scalar; only the force it produces on a surface has a direction.
distractor_logic: Confuses the weight of the liquid (which acts downward) with pressure, which is a scalar and acts equally in every direction
No direction is preferred for pressure in a fluid at rest
Pressure exists at every point inside the liquid, not just at the walls

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: According to Archimedes' principle, the buoyant force on a body immersed in a fluid equals
options: the weight of the fluid displaced by the body
the weight of the fluid in the container
the volume of the body multiplied by its own density
questions.explanation:
When a body is immersed, it pushes aside (displaces) some fluid.

The buoyant force on the body is equal to the weight of that displaced fluid: \( F_B=\rho_{fluid}V_{displaced}g \).

It acts vertically upward.
questions.hint: Buoyancy is about the fluid pushed aside, not the body itself.
distractor_logic: Equals the body's weight only in the special case of floating
Only the displaced portion of the fluid matters, not everything in the container
Uses the body's density; the buoyant force depends on the fluid's density and the displaced volume

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: A body of volume \( 0.002 \) m\(^3\) is fully submerged in water (density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\)). With \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the buoyant force on it is
questions.explanation:
For a fully submerged body the displaced volume is the whole volume of the body.

\( F_B=\rho_{fluid}Vg=1000\times0.002\times10=20 \) N.
questions.hint: \( F_B=\rho_{fluid}V_{displaced}g \).
distractor_logic: Drops a factor of ten in the arithmetic
Uses a volume ten times too large
Assumes a submerged body experiences no upthrust; buoyancy acts whenever fluid is displaced

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: A wooden block of density \( 600 \) kg/m\(^3\) floats in water of density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\). The fraction of its volume that is submerged is
questions.explanation:
For a floating body, weight equals buoyant force: \( \rho_{object}V_{object}g=\rho_{fluid}V_{displaced}g \).

So \( \dfrac{V_{displaced}}{V_{object}}=\dfrac{\rho_{object}}{\rho_{fluid}}=\dfrac{600}{1000}=\dfrac{3}{5} \).
questions.hint: Fraction submerged = density of object divided by density of fluid.
distractor_logic: Treats the whole block as submerged, but a floating block displaces only enough water to balance its weight
Gives the fraction above water instead of the submerged fraction
Assumes a floating block is entirely above water; part must be submerged to displace water

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: A piece of iron (density about \( 7800 \) kg/m\(^3\)) sinks in water (density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\)) but floats on mercury (density \( 13600 \) kg/m\(^3\)) because
options: mercury exerts no buoyant force on iron
iron is less dense than both water and mercury
mercury is a metal, so it repels other metals
iron is denser than water but less dense than mercury
questions.explanation:
A body floats when its density is less than the fluid's density and sinks when it is greater.

Iron (7800) is denser than water (1000), so it sinks in water.

Iron is less dense than mercury (13600), so mercury can supply enough buoyant force for iron to float.
questions.hint: Compare the body's density with each fluid's density.
distractor_logic: Mercury exerts a large buoyant force; that is exactly why iron floats on it
Iron is denser than water, which is why it sinks there
Floating has nothing to do with both being metals; it is governed by density comparison

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: A stone weighs 50 N in air. When fully immersed in water the buoyant force on it is 20 N. Its apparent weight in water is
questions.explanation:
Apparent weight = true weight minus buoyant force.

\( W_{app}=50-20=30 \) N.
questions.hint: Buoyancy pushes up, so the stone feels lighter.
distractor_logic: Adds the buoyant force instead of subtracting it; buoyancy acts upward and reduces the apparent weight
Reports the buoyant force itself as the apparent weight
Assumes immersion does not change the weight reading

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: The buoyant force on a fully submerged body acts through
options: the lowest point of the body
the centre of gravity of the displaced fluid (the centre of buoyancy)
the highest point of the body
the point of the body nearest the container wall
questions.explanation:
Buoyant force is the resultant of the pressure forces over the entire surface of the body.

This resultant acts at the centre of gravity of the fluid that has been displaced, called the centre of buoyancy.

For a uniform fully submerged body this coincides with its geometric centre.
questions.hint: Imagine the displaced fluid put back: where does its weight act?
distractor_logic: Buoyancy is a resultant of pressure over the whole surface, not a force at the bottom point
Not the top point either; it acts at the centroid of the displaced volume
The container wall has no bearing on where buoyancy acts

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: For a body floating at rest on the surface of a liquid, which statement is correct?
options: The buoyant force is greater than the weight of the body
The buoyant force is less than the weight of the body
The buoyant force is equal to the weight of the body
The buoyant force is zero because the body is not fully submerged
questions.explanation:
A floating body is in equilibrium, so the net vertical force is zero.

The only vertical forces are its weight (down) and the buoyant force (up), so they must be equal.

The body sinks just enough to displace liquid whose weight equals its own.
questions.hint: Equilibrium means the forces balance.
distractor_logic: A net upward force would make the body accelerate upward, not float at rest
A net downward force would make the body sink further
A partially submerged body still displaces liquid, so buoyancy is not zero

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: The buoyant force on a body completely submerged in an incompressible liquid depends on
options: the depth to which the body is submerged
the density of the liquid and the volume of the body
questions.explanation:
\( F_B=\rho_{fluid}V_{displaced}g \).

For a fully submerged body, \( V_{displaced} \) is the body's volume, and \( \rho_{fluid} \) is the liquid's density.

Neither the depth nor the body's own density or mass appears in the expression.
questions.hint: Read the variables in \( F_B=\rho_{fluid}Vg \).
distractor_logic: In an incompressible liquid the buoyant force is the same at all depths
The body's density affects whether it sinks or floats, not the size of the buoyant force on a fully submerged body
Two bodies of the same volume but different mass experience the same buoyant force

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: Water flows through a pipe of cross-sectional area 4 cm\(^2\) at 2 m/s. The pipe narrows to 2 cm\(^2\). The speed of water in the narrow part is
questions.explanation:
By the equation of continuity, \( A_1v_1=A_2v_2 \).

\( v_2=\dfrac{A_1v_1}{A_2}=\dfrac{4\times2}{2}=4 \) m/s.
questions.hint: Same volume per second through every cross-section.
distractor_logic: Inverts the continuity relation; a smaller area means a larger speed
Assumes the speed is unchanged; the same volume per second must pass through a smaller area
Applies the area ratio twice

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: Bernoulli's principle is a consequence of the conservation of
questions.explanation:
Bernoulli's equation, \( P+\tfrac12\rho v^2+\rho gh=\text{constant} \), is obtained by applying the work-energy theorem to a fluid element moving along a streamline.

Each term is an energy per unit volume: pressure energy, kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy.
questions.hint: Each term in the equation is an energy per unit volume.
distractor_logic: Mass conservation gives the equation of continuity, not Bernoulli's equation
Bernoulli's equation is a work-energy statement, not a momentum balance
Angular momentum plays no role in streamline flow along a pipe

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: Water flows steadily through a horizontal pipe that narrows. In the narrow section, compared with the wide section,
options: the speed is higher and the pressure is higher
the speed is lower and the pressure is higher
the speed is higher and the pressure is lower
the speed and pressure are both unchanged
questions.explanation:
Continuity: \( A_1v_1=A_2v_2 \), so the smaller area has the larger speed.

Bernoulli (horizontal, so no height term): \( P+\tfrac12\rho v^2=\text{constant} \). A larger speed means a smaller pressure.

The narrow section therefore has higher speed and lower pressure.
questions.hint: Continuity fixes the speed; Bernoulli then fixes the pressure.
distractor_logic: Intuitive guess that pressure 'builds up' where the pipe narrows; Bernoulli's equation shows faster flow means lower pressure
Gets the speed backward; continuity requires the speed to increase where the area decreases
Ignores both continuity and Bernoulli's equation

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: In steady (streamline) flow of a fluid,
options: every fluid particle has the same speed
the fluid moves in a straight line only
the pressure is the same at all points
the velocity of the fluid at any given point remains constant in time
questions.explanation:
In steady flow, the velocity at each point of the fluid is constant in time, although it may differ from point to point.

Every particle passing a given point follows the same path, called a streamline, and streamlines never cross.
questions.hint: Steady means 'not changing with time' at a fixed location.
distractor_logic: Different points can have different velocities; steadiness means each point's velocity does not change with time
Streamlines can be curved; 'streamline' does not mean 'straight line'
Pressure generally varies from point to point in a flow

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: The equation of continuity for an incompressible fluid follows from the conservation of
questions.explanation:
For an incompressible fluid, the mass entering one end of a tube of flow per second must equal the mass leaving the other end.

Since density is constant, this means the volume flow rate \( Av \) is the same at every cross-section: \( A_1v_1=A_2v_2 \).
questions.hint: What must be the same at both ends of a tube of flow each second?
distractor_logic: Energy conservation is what gives Bernoulli's equation
Momentum conservation is not the basis of the continuity relation
Angular momentum is unrelated to the volume flow through a tube

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: Each term in Bernoulli's equation \( P+\tfrac12\rho v^2+\rho gh \) has the dimensions of
questions.explanation:
\( P \) is force per area, which equals (force times distance) per volume, i.e. energy per unit volume.

\( \tfrac12\rho v^2 \) is kinetic energy per unit volume and \( \rho gh \) is potential energy per unit volume.

All three terms share the units of pressure, which are the same as J/m\(^3\).
questions.hint: Check the units of pressure: N/m\(^2\) equals J/m\(^3\).
distractor_logic: Pressure is force per area, not force
Dividing each term by density would give energy per mass; as written, the terms are per volume
No term contains a rate of change with time

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: Water moves at 3 m/s through a pipe of cross-sectional area 10 cm\(^2\). The volume flow rate is
questions.hint: Convert the area to m\(^2\) before multiplying.
distractor_logic: Forgets to convert cm\(^2\) to m\(^2\)
Converts cm\(^2\) using a factor of 100 instead of 10000
Applies the cm-to-m conversion twice

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: The Reynolds number for the flow of a liquid in a pipe is found to be about 500. The flow is
options: impossible, since the Reynolds number must exceed 1000
questions.explanation:
The Reynolds number \( Re=\dfrac{\rho vd}{\eta} \) is a dimensionless number used to classify flow.

Flow is laminar for \( Re \) below about 1000, turbulent above about 2000, and unstable in between.

A value of 500 indicates laminar flow.
questions.hint: Below 1000: laminar. Above 2000: turbulent.
distractor_logic: Turbulence sets in at Reynolds numbers above about 2000
Reynolds number classifies laminar versus turbulent, not steady versus unsteady
The Reynolds number can take any positive value; small values mean smooth flow

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: Viscosity of a fluid is best described as
options: the internal friction between adjacent layers of the fluid moving at different speeds
the force of attraction between the fluid and the walls of the container
the tendency of the fluid surface to contract
the pressure exerted by the fluid on the container
questions.explanation:
When one layer of a fluid slides over another, each layer exerts a tangential (shear) force opposing the relative motion.

This internal friction is called viscosity. Honey has a large viscosity; water has a small one.
questions.hint: Think of fluid layers rubbing against each other.
distractor_logic: Adhesion to the walls is a different effect; viscosity acts between fluid layers
Surface contraction is surface tension, not viscosity
Pressure is unrelated to the friction between moving layers

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: The SI unit of the coefficient of viscosity \( \eta \) is
questions.explanation:
From \( F=\eta A\dfrac{dv}{dx} \), \( \eta=\dfrac{F}{A}\cdot\dfrac{dx}{dv} \).

Units: \( \dfrac{\text{N}}{\text{m}^2}\cdot\dfrac{\text{m}}{\text{m/s}} \) = N s/m\(^2\) = Pa s.
questions.hint: Rearrange Newton's law of viscosity to isolate \( \eta \).
distractor_logic: N/m is the unit of surface tension
N/m\(^2\) is the unit of pressure or stress; viscosity has an additional unit of time
m\(^2\)/s is the unit of kinematic viscosity, not the coefficient of viscosity

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: According to Stokes' law, the viscous drag on a small sphere of radius \( r \) moving with speed \( v \) through a fluid of viscosity \( \eta \) is
questions.explanation:
Stokes showed that the drag on a sphere moving slowly through a viscous fluid is \( F=6\pi\eta rv \).

It is proportional to the viscosity, the radius, and the speed, each to the first power.
questions.hint: Drag is linear in radius and in speed.
distractor_logic: Uses the square of the radius; the drag depends on the first power of \( r \)
Uses the wrong numerical factor
Uses the square of the speed; Stokes' drag is proportional to the first power of \( v \)

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: The terminal velocity of a small sphere falling through a viscous fluid is proportional to
options: the cube of the radius of the sphere
the square of the radius of the sphere
questions.explanation:
At terminal velocity, weight minus buoyancy equals viscous drag: \( \tfrac43\pi r^3(\rho_{body}-\rho_{fluid})g=6\pi\eta rv_t \).

Solving, \( v_t=\dfrac{2r^2(\rho_{body}-\rho_{fluid})g}{9\eta} \), which is proportional to \( r^2 \).
questions.hint: Balance the net downward force against Stokes' drag.
distractor_logic: The weight-minus-buoyancy grows as \( r^3 \) while the drag grows as \( r \), so the speed grows as \( r^2 \), not \( r \)
Cubing overstates the dependence; the drag's linear growth in \( r \) reduces the power from 3 to 2
Terminal velocity is inversely proportional to viscosity, not proportional to it

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: When a liquid is heated, its viscosity
questions.explanation:
In liquids, viscosity arises mainly from intermolecular attraction between layers.

Heating gives molecules more kinetic energy and weakens the effect of these attractions, so the liquid flows more easily and its viscosity decreases.

Gases behave oppositely: their viscosity increases with temperature.
questions.hint: Warm honey flows more easily than cold honey.
distractor_logic: This is the behaviour of gases, whose viscosity rises with temperature
Viscosity of liquids is strongly temperature dependent, as anyone warming honey can see
No such reversal occurs for ordinary liquids

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: According to Poiseuille's equation, if the radius of a tube is doubled (with the same pressure difference, length and liquid), the volume flow rate becomes
questions.explanation:
Poiseuille's equation: \( Q=\dfrac{\pi Pr^4}{8\eta l} \), so the flow rate is proportional to \( r^4 \).

Doubling \( r \) multiplies the flow rate by \( 2^4=16 \).
questions.hint: Flow rate goes as the fourth power of the radius.
distractor_logic: Assumes flow rate is proportional to the radius
Assumes flow rate scales with the area, i.e. the square of the radius
Uses the cube of the radius

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: A sphere falling through a viscous fluid reaches its terminal velocity when
options: the net force on it becomes zero
questions.explanation:
As the sphere speeds up, the viscous drag (proportional to speed) grows.

Eventually drag plus buoyancy equals the weight, the net force is zero, and the sphere continues at a constant speed called the terminal velocity.
questions.hint: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, hence zero net force.
distractor_logic: Drag is largest at terminal velocity; it is what balances the weight
Buoyancy is constant throughout the fall and does not vanish
Weight is constant; it is balanced, not removed

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: A sphere of radius 1 mm moves at 0.1 m/s through a liquid of viscosity \( \eta=1 \) Pa s. The viscous drag on it is
questions.explanation:
Stokes' law: \( F=6\pi\eta rv \).

\( F=6\pi\times1\times10^{-3}\times0.1=6\pi\times10^{-4} \) N.
questions.hint: Convert the radius to metres first.
distractor_logic: Forgets to convert millimetres to metres
Uses the square of the radius
Uses the wrong numerical factor in Stokes' law

questions.topic: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
questions.question: The SI unit of surface tension is
questions.explanation:
Surface tension is the force per unit length acting along an imaginary line drawn on the liquid surface: \( T=\dfrac{F}{l} \).

Its SI unit is N/m, which is the same as J/m\(^2\) (energy per unit area).
questions.hint: Force per unit length, or equivalently energy per unit area.
distractor_logic: This is the unit of pressure
This is the unit of work or torque
This is energy per volume, the unit of pressure again; surface tension is energy per area

questions.topic: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
questions.question: The excess pressure inside a liquid drop of radius \( r \) and surface tension \( T \) is
questions.explanation:
A liquid drop has a single free surface. Balancing the surface-tension force against the excess pressure gives \( P_{excess}=\dfrac{2T}{r} \).

A soap bubble has an inner and an outer surface, so its excess pressure is \( \dfrac{4T}{r} \).
questions.hint: One surface for a drop, two for a bubble.
distractor_logic: This is the excess pressure inside a soap bubble, which has two surfaces; a drop has only one
Misses the factor 2 that comes from the curved surface in two directions
Wrong dependence on the radius; excess pressure varies as the inverse of \( r \)

questions.topic: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
questions.question: Water rises in a clean glass capillary tube because
options: the angle of contact is obtuse
the angle of contact between water and glass is acute (less than 90 degrees)
the atmospheric pressure inside the tube is lower
questions.explanation:
Water wets glass: the adhesive forces between water and glass exceed the cohesive forces in water, so the angle of contact is acute and the meniscus is concave.

The pressure just below the concave meniscus is less than atmospheric, so water is pushed up the tube until the column's weight balances this pressure difference: \( h=\dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{\rho gr} \).
questions.hint: Concave meniscus, acute contact angle, liquid rises.
distractor_logic: An obtuse angle (as for mercury on glass) causes depression, not rise
Density comparison with the solid is irrelevant; wetting behaviour decides the rise
Atmospheric pressure is the same inside and outside an open tube

questions.topic: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
questions.question: Surface tension of a liquid arises mainly from
options: adhesive forces between the liquid and the container
the pressure of the atmosphere on the liquid surface
cohesive forces between the molecules of the liquid
questions.explanation:
Molecules in the bulk are pulled equally in all directions by their neighbours, but molecules at the surface have neighbours only on one side.

Surface molecules therefore have extra potential energy, and the surface tends to shrink to minimise this energy. This is surface tension.
questions.hint: Why does a surface molecule differ from one in the bulk?
distractor_logic: Adhesion affects the angle of contact, not the surface tension itself
Surface tension exists even in a vacuum
Viscosity is a resistance to flow, unrelated to surface energy

questions.topic: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
questions.question: A liquid film of surface tension \( T \) has its surface area increased by \( \Delta A \) at constant temperature. The work done is
options: \( 2T\,\Delta A \) for every film, regardless of the number of surfaces
questions.explanation:
Surface tension equals the surface energy per unit area.

Increasing the total surface area by \( \Delta A \) stores an energy \( T\,\Delta A \), which is the work that must be done.
questions.hint: Surface tension is surface energy per unit area.
distractor_logic: Inverts the relationship; work grows with area
The factor 2 applies only when \( \Delta A \) counts one side of a film that has two free surfaces; in general work equals \( T \) times the total surface area created
Work is linear in the area change, not quadratic

questions.topic: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
questions.question: A water drop has radius 1 mm. With surface tension \( T=0.07 \) N/m, the excess pressure inside the drop is
questions.explanation:
For a drop (one surface), \( P_{excess}=\dfrac{2T}{r} \).

\( P_{excess}=\dfrac{2\times0.07}{10^{-3}}=140 \) Pa.
questions.hint: Drop: two-T-over-r. Convert the radius to metres.
distractor_logic: Uses \( 4T/r \), the soap-bubble formula, for a single-surface drop
Uses \( T/r \), omitting the factor 2
Forgets to convert millimetres to metres

questions.topic: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
questions.question: When a glass capillary tube is dipped into mercury, the mercury level inside the tube is depressed below the outside level because
options: mercury is too heavy to rise
the angle of contact of mercury with glass is obtuse and the meniscus is convex
the tube is too narrow for mercury atoms
questions.explanation:
Mercury does not wet glass: cohesion in mercury exceeds adhesion to glass, so the contact angle is obtuse (about 140 degrees) and the meniscus is convex.

The pressure just below a convex meniscus is greater than atmospheric, pushing the mercury down inside the tube.
questions.hint: Convex meniscus means the liquid is pushed down, not up.
distractor_logic: Weight alone does not explain depression; the direction of the surface-tension force does
Mercury has a large surface tension; it is the obtuse contact angle that matters
Atomic size plays no role in capillary action at this scale

questions.topic: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
questions.question: As the temperature of a liquid increases, its surface tension generally
options: becomes infinite at the boiling point
questions.explanation:
Surface tension comes from intermolecular attraction. Raising the temperature increases molecular kinetic energy and reduces the net inward pull on surface molecules.

So the surface tension decreases with rising temperature, reaching zero at the critical temperature.
questions.hint: Hot water wets and spreads more easily than cold water.
distractor_logic: Higher temperature weakens intermolecular attraction, lowering surface tension
Surface tension is noticeably temperature dependent
Surface tension actually falls to zero at the critical temperature

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: A U-tube mercury manometer is connected to a gas cylinder. The mercury level on the open side stands 20 cm higher than on the gas side. If atmospheric pressure is 76 cmHg, the absolute pressure of the gas is
questions.explanation:
The open side stands higher, so the gas pushes the mercury down on its side: the gas pressure exceeds atmospheric pressure.

Gauge pressure of the gas = 20 cmHg.

Absolute pressure = atmospheric + gauge = 76 + 20 = 96 cmHg.
questions.hint: Which side is being pushed down? That side has the higher pressure.
distractor_logic: Reports only the gauge pressure (the mercury difference) instead of adding atmospheric pressure
Subtracts the difference from atmospheric pressure; the open-side level is higher, so the gas pressure is greater than atmospheric
Adds the 20 cm difference twice

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: In a hydraulic press the area of the large piston is 100 times that of the small piston. If the small piston is pushed down through 100 cm, the large piston rises by
questions.explanation:
The liquid is incompressible, so the volume pushed out under the small piston equals the volume that lifts the large piston: \( A_1d_1=A_2d_2 \).

\( d_2=d_1\dfrac{A_1}{A_2}=100\times\dfrac{1}{100}=1 \) cm.

The force is multiplied by 100 but the distance is divided by 100, so work is conserved.
questions.hint: Volume of fluid displaced on both sides is equal.
distractor_logic: Assumes both pistons move equally; the fluid volume displaced must be the same, so the larger piston moves less
Uses the square root of the area ratio
Inverts the ratio, making the large piston move more

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: A tank contains a 1 m layer of oil (density \( 800 \) kg/m\(^3\)) floating on 2 m of water (density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\)). With \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the gauge pressure at the bottom of the tank is
questions.explanation:
Each layer contributes its own \( h\rho g \).

Oil: \( 1\times800\times10=8000 \) Pa. Water: \( 2\times1000\times10=20000 \) Pa.

Gauge pressure at the bottom \( =8000+20000=28000 \) Pa \( =2.8\times10^{4} \) Pa.
questions.hint: Add the hydrostatic contribution of each layer separately.
distractor_logic: Treats the whole 3 m column as water
Treats the whole 3 m column as oil
Adds atmospheric pressure of \( 1.0\times10^{5} \) Pa to the gauge value; gauge pressure was asked

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: The thrust exerted by water on a dam depends on
options: the length of the reservoir behind the dam
the total volume of water stored
both the height and the horizontal extent of the reservoir equally
the height of water behind the dam, not on the length of the reservoir
questions.explanation:
Pressure at a depth \( h \) is \( h\rho g \) and depends only on \( h \) and \( \rho \).

The horizontal extent of the reservoir does not appear in the expression, so a long reservoir and a short one of the same depth exert the same pressure on the dam.

That is why dams are built thicker at the bottom, where the depth is greatest.
questions.hint: Hydrostatic pressure cares about depth, not about how much water lies behind.
distractor_logic: Pressure at a depth is independent of how far the water extends horizontally
Total volume does not set pressure; only depth does
Only depth enters the hydrostatic pressure; the horizontal extent is irrelevant

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: Two points A and B lie at the same horizontal level inside a liquid at rest in an irregularly shaped vessel. The vessel is much wider near A than near B. The pressure difference between A and B is
options: greater at A because more liquid lies above it
greater at B because the liquid is confined in a narrower part
impossible to determine without knowing the vessel's shape
questions.explanation:
In a connected liquid at rest, pressure depends only on depth below the free surface.

Points at the same horizontal level are at the same depth, so their pressures are equal.

If they were not, the liquid would flow between them, contradicting rest.
questions.hint: If the pressures differed, the liquid would start to flow horizontally.
distractor_logic: The amount of liquid overhead does not matter; depth alone fixes pressure
Confinement in a narrow region does not raise pressure in a fluid at rest
The shape is irrelevant: equal depth in the same connected liquid means equal pressure

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: A diver is at a depth of 20 m in sea water of density \( 1030 \) kg/m\(^3\). Taking \( P_{atm}=1.0\times10^{5} \) Pa and \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the absolute pressure on the diver is
questions.explanation:
Gauge pressure \( =h\rho g=20\times1030\times10=2.06\times10^{5} \) Pa.

Absolute pressure \( =P_{atm}+h\rho g=1.0\times10^{5}+2.06\times10^{5}=3.06\times10^{5} \) Pa.
questions.hint: Absolute = atmospheric + hydrostatic.
distractor_logic: Gives only the gauge pressure, leaving out atmospheric pressure
Uses the density of fresh water (1000) instead of sea water (1030)
Adds atmospheric pressure twice

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: A mercury barometer is placed in a lift. When the lift accelerates upward, the barometer reading (height of the mercury column)
questions.explanation:
In a lift accelerating upward with acceleration \( a \), the effective gravity is \( g+a \).

Atmospheric pressure is unchanged, and it balances the column: \( P_{atm}=h\rho(g+a) \).

Since \( g+a>g \), the column height \( h \) must decrease.
questions.hint: Write \( P_{atm}=h\rho g_{eff} \) and ask what happens to \( g_{eff} \).
distractor_logic: Assumes the heavier effective weight of mercury pushes the column up; in fact a heavier column needs less height to balance the same pressure
Ignores that the effective gravity acting on the mercury column has changed
Only a freely falling lift would make the column meaningless; upward acceleration merely increases effective gravity

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: Vessels A (wide, straight-sided) and B (narrow at the top, widening to the same base area as A) are filled with water to the same height. Compare the force on the base of each vessel.
options: The force on the base of A is greater because A holds more water
The force on the base of B is greater because its top is narrower
The forces are equal only if the weights of water are equal
The forces on the bases are equal, even though the weights of water in the vessels differ
questions.explanation:
Pressure at the base of each vessel is \( h\rho g \), the same for both since the depth is the same.

Force on the base = pressure times base area, and the base areas are equal, so the forces are equal.

The weights of water differ; the extra or missing weight is accounted for by the reaction of the slanting walls. This is the hydrostatic paradox.
questions.hint: Base force = (pressure at base) times (base area).
distractor_logic: Force on the base is pressure times base area; pressure depends on depth, not on how much water is stored
A narrow top does not raise the pressure at the base
The force on the base need not equal the weight of the water; the difference is balanced by the vessel walls

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: Ice of density \( 900 \) kg/m\(^3\) floats in water of density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\). The fraction of the ice that is above the water surface is
questions.explanation:
Submerged fraction \( =\dfrac{\rho_{ice}}{\rho_{water}}=\dfrac{900}{1000}=\dfrac{9}{10} \).

Fraction above water \( =1-\dfrac{9}{10}=\dfrac{1}{10} \).
questions.hint: First find the submerged fraction, then subtract from one.
distractor_logic: Gives the submerged fraction instead of the fraction above the surface
Assumes ice is fully submerged; a body less dense than water floats partly above it
Divides by the ice density instead of the water density

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: A wooden block of volume \( 0.5 \) m\(^3\) and density \( 800 \) kg/m\(^3\) floats in water of density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\). With \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the buoyant force acting on the block is
questions.explanation:
A floating block displaces only enough water to balance its own weight, so \( F_B= \) weight of the block.

Weight \( =\rho_{block}Vg=800\times0.5\times10=4000 \) N.

Check: the submerged volume is \( 0.4 \) m\(^3\), and \( 1000\times0.4\times10=4000 \) N.
questions.hint: For a floating body, buoyant force equals weight; don't use the whole volume.
distractor_logic: Uses the block's full volume as the displaced volume; only the submerged 80 percent displaces water
Gives the difference between the two calculations rather than the buoyant force
Confuses the density values in the calculation, effectively using 1600 kg/m\(^3\)

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: A body of mass 5 kg and volume \( 0.01 \) m\(^3\) is held fully submerged in water (density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\)) by a string tied to the bottom of the tank. With \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the tension in the string is
questions.explanation:
Buoyant force \( =\rho_{water}Vg=1000\times0.01\times10=100 \) N.

Weight \( =5\times10=50 \) N.

The body tends to rise, so the string pulls it down: \( T=F_B-W=100-50=50 \) N.
questions.hint: Compare the upthrust with the weight; the string makes up the difference.
distractor_logic: Reports the buoyant force itself rather than the excess of buoyancy over weight
Adds weight and buoyancy instead of subtracting
Assumes the body is in equilibrium without the string; since it is lighter than the displaced water, the string must hold it down

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: The same solid body is fully submerged first in water (density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\)) and then in oil (density \( 800 \) kg/m\(^3\)). The ratio of the buoyant force in water to that in oil is
options: dependent on the density of the body
questions.explanation:
For full submersion the displaced volume is the body's volume \( V \) in both cases.

\( \dfrac{F_{water}}{F_{oil}}=\dfrac{\rho_{water}Vg}{\rho_{oil}Vg}=\dfrac{1000}{800}=\dfrac{5}{4} \).
questions.hint: Same displaced volume, different fluid densities.
distractor_logic: The buoyant force depends on the fluid density, so it changes from one fluid to another
Inverts the ratio; the denser fluid gives the larger buoyant force
For a fully submerged body the buoyant force is set by the fluid's density and the body's volume, not the body's density

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: A body weighs 100 N in air and 80 N when fully immersed in water (density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\)). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the density of the body is
questions.explanation:
Loss of weight = buoyant force \( =100-80=20 \) N, so \( \rho_{water}Vg=20 \) and \( V=\dfrac{20}{1000\times10}=0.002 \) m\(^3\).

Mass \( =\dfrac{100}{10}=10 \) kg.

Density \( =\dfrac{10}{0.002}=5000 \) kg/m\(^3\).
questions.hint: Loss of weight in water gives the volume; weight in air gives the mass.
distractor_logic: Drops a factor of ten when converting the loss of weight to volume
Uses the apparent weight (80 N) instead of the true weight (100 N) to find the mass
Assumes a body immersed in water must have the density of water

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: A boat carrying a large stone floats in a small pond. The stone is dropped into the pond and sinks to the bottom. The water level of the pond
options: first rises, then returns to the original level
questions.explanation:
In the boat, the stone floats (with the boat) and displaces water whose weight equals the stone's weight. Since the stone is denser than water, this displaced volume is larger than the stone's own volume.

At the bottom of the pond, the stone displaces only its own volume.

The displaced volume decreases, so the water level falls.
questions.hint: Compare the water displaced while floating with the water displaced while sunk.
distractor_logic: Assumes the sunken stone displaces more water than before; in the boat it displaced water equal to its weight, which is more than its volume
The displaced volume changes because the stone stops floating (via the boat) and starts sinking
The final state is different from the initial one, so the level does not return

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: Two balls of the same material and the same mass are fully submerged in water; one is solid and the other is hollow. Which experiences the larger buoyant force?
options: The solid ball, because it is denser
Both experience the same buoyant force because their masses are equal
The hollow ball, because it has the larger volume
The solid ball, because it sinks faster
questions.explanation:
Same mass and same material means the same amount of solid material, but the hollow ball encloses extra empty space, giving it the larger total volume.

Fully submerged, \( F_B=\rho_{water}Vg \), so the larger volume gives the larger buoyant force.
questions.hint: Which ball pushes aside more water?
distractor_logic: Buoyancy depends on displaced volume, not on how dense the object is
Equal mass does not mean equal volume; the hollow ball is bigger
How fast a body sinks is a consequence, not a cause, of the buoyant force

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: A block of density \( 750 \) kg/m\(^3\) floats in oil of density \( 900 \) kg/m\(^3\). The fraction of the block submerged is
questions.explanation:
Fraction submerged \( =\dfrac{\rho_{block}}{\rho_{oil}}=\dfrac{750}{900}=\dfrac{5}{6} \).

Only the fluid the block actually floats in matters.
questions.hint: Use the density of the fluid the block is floating in.
distractor_logic: Inverts the density ratio; a fraction submerged cannot exceed 1
Gives the fraction above the surface instead of the submerged fraction
Uses the density of water (1000) instead of the oil the block actually floats in

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: Water flows through a horizontal pipe. At a point where the diameter of the pipe is halved, the speed of the water becomes
questions.explanation:
Area is proportional to the square of the diameter, so halving the diameter makes the area one-quarter.

Continuity, \( A_1v_1=A_2v_2 \), then gives \( v_2=4v_1 \).

Pressure does not enter this calculation at all; continuity alone links speed to area.
questions.hint: Halving the diameter quarters the area.
distractor_logic: Uses the diameter ratio instead of the area ratio; area scales with the square of the diameter
Inverts the relation; a smaller area gives a larger speed
Both inverts the relation and forgets to square the diameter ratio

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: Water (density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\)) flows through a horizontal pipe. Its speed is 2 m/s at a wide section and 4 m/s at a narrow section. The pressure at the wide section exceeds that at the narrow section by
questions.explanation:
Horizontal pipe, so Bernoulli's equation reduces to \( P_1+\tfrac12\rho v_1^2=P_2+\tfrac12\rho v_2^2 \).

\( P_1-P_2=\tfrac12\rho(v_2^2-v_1^2)=\tfrac12\times1000\times(16-4)=6000 \) Pa.
questions.hint: Difference of squares, not square of the difference.
distractor_logic: Uses \( \tfrac12\rho(v_2-v_1)^2 \) instead of \( \tfrac12\rho(v_2^2-v_1^2) \)
Omits the factor of one-half
Uses the speed difference squared and also doubles the result; the correct expression involves the difference of squares

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: In a venturi meter, the pressure at the constricted throat compared with the pressure in the wider inlet section is
options: higher, because the fluid is compressed there
the same, because the pipe is horizontal
lower, because the fluid moves faster there
higher, because the fluid moves faster there
questions.explanation:
Continuity makes the fluid speed up in the narrow throat.

With no height change, Bernoulli's equation gives \( P+\tfrac12\rho v^2=\text{constant} \), so higher speed means lower pressure.

The measured pressure drop at the throat is used to find the flow speed.
questions.hint: The throat is where the streamlines crowd together.
distractor_logic: The fluid is incompressible; the pressure drops because of the higher speed, not because of compression
A horizontal pipe removes the height term but the speed term still changes
Faster flow corresponds to lower, not higher, pressure along a streamline

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: An aeroplane wing is shaped so that air travels faster over its upper surface than under its lower surface. This produces lift because
options: the faster air above the wing exerts more pressure on it
air is compressed under the wing
the wing pushes the air upward
the pressure above the wing is lower than the pressure below it
questions.explanation:
By Bernoulli's principle, the faster-moving air over the upper surface has lower pressure than the slower air below.

The pressure difference times the wing area gives a net upward force, the dynamic lift.
questions.hint: Fast air, low pressure; slow air, high pressure.
distractor_logic: Higher speed means lower pressure, not more pressure
At these speeds air is treated as incompressible; the effect is a speed-pressure trade-off
This describes a different mechanism (reaction); the Bernoulli explanation is a pressure difference across the wing

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: A large tank open to the atmosphere has a small hole in its side 5 m below the water surface. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the speed with which water comes out of the hole is
questions.explanation:
Torricelli's law (from Bernoulli, with the tank surface nearly at rest and both surfaces at atmospheric pressure): \( v=\sqrt{2gh} \).

\( v=\sqrt{2\times10\times5}=\sqrt{100}=10 \) m/s.
questions.hint: Same as the speed of a body falling freely through the same height.
distractor_logic: Takes the speed equal to the depth in metres, dropping the factor \( 2g \) and the square root
Forgets to take the square root of \( 2gh \)
Uses \( gh \) without the factor 2 and without the square root

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: The Reynolds number for flow in a pipe is \( Re=\dfrac{\rho vd}{\eta} \). If the flow speed is doubled while the pipe and the liquid are unchanged, the Reynolds number
questions.explanation:
\( Re \) is directly proportional to the speed \( v \) when \( \rho \), \( d \) and \( \eta \) are held fixed.

Doubling \( v \) doubles \( Re \). This is why fast flow tends to become turbulent.
questions.hint: Which quantities in the formula change?
distractor_logic: Reynolds number depends directly on the speed
The dependence on speed is linear, not quadratic
Speed appears in the numerator, so a larger speed gives a larger Reynolds number

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: A ball spinning as it moves through air curves sideways from its straight-line path. This happens because
options: the ball's spin increases its weight on one side
air is denser on the spinning side
air moves faster on one side of the ball than on the other, creating a pressure difference
gravity acts differently on a spinning ball
questions.explanation:
The spinning surface drags air along with it, so on one side the air speed relative to the ball is higher and on the other side lower.

By Bernoulli's principle the faster side has lower pressure, so there is a net sideways force (the Magnus effect) that curves the path.
questions.hint: Bernoulli again: unequal speeds mean unequal pressures.
distractor_logic: Spin does not change the ball's weight
Air density is essentially uniform around the ball; the speed of the air relative to the surface differs
Gravity is unaffected by spin

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: Two boats moving side by side in the same direction in still water are observed to be pulled toward each other. This is because
options: the water between them is at rest, so the pressure between them is higher
gravity between the two boats attracts them
the boats create waves that push them together
the water between them flows faster, so the pressure between them is lower than on the outer sides
questions.explanation:
The water between the two boats must pass through a narrower channel, so by continuity it moves faster.

By Bernoulli's principle the faster water has lower pressure.

The higher pressure on the outer sides of the boats pushes them together.
questions.hint: Narrow channel: faster water, lower pressure.
distractor_logic: The water between the boats is squeezed into a narrower channel and speeds up; it is not at rest
Gravitational attraction between boats is far too small to matter
The effect is explained by the pressure drop of fast-moving water, not by waves

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: A steel sphere of radius 3 mm and density \( 3000 \) kg/m\(^3\) falls through a liquid of density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\) and viscosity \( \eta=0.8 \) Pa s. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), its terminal velocity is
questions.explanation:
\( v_t=\dfrac{2r^2(\rho_{body}-\rho_{fluid})g}{9\eta} \).

\( r^2=(3\times10^{-3})^2=9\times10^{-6} \) m\(^2\); density difference \( =2000 \) kg/m\(^3\).

\( v_t=\dfrac{2\times9\times10^{-6}\times2000\times10}{9\times0.8}=\dfrac{0.36}{7.2}=0.05 \) m/s.
questions.hint: Use the difference of densities, and the coefficient two-ninths.
distractor_logic: Uses the sphere's density alone (3000) instead of the density difference (2000), ignoring buoyancy
Uses a coefficient of \( \tfrac19 \) instead of \( \tfrac29 \)
Slips a factor of ten in the unit conversion of the radius

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: In Poiseuille flow, the radius of the tube is halved and its length is doubled, with the pressure difference unchanged. The volume flow rate becomes
questions.explanation:
\( Q\propto\dfrac{r^4}{l} \).

Halving \( r \) gives a factor \( \dfrac{1}{16} \); doubling \( l \) gives a further factor \( \dfrac12 \).

Combined: \( \dfrac{1}{32} \).
questions.hint: Fourth power of radius, inverse first power of length.
distractor_logic: Accounts for the radius change but forgets that doubling the length halves the flow
Uses the cube of the radius and ignores the length
Uses the square of the radius and ignores the length

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: Two spheres of the same material have radii in the ratio 1 : 2. They fall through the same viscous liquid. The ratio of their terminal velocities is
questions.explanation:
\( v_t\propto r^2 \) when the densities and viscosity are the same.

\( \dfrac{v_1}{v_2}=\dfrac{1^2}{2^2}=\dfrac14 \).
questions.hint: Terminal velocity scales as radius squared.
distractor_logic: Takes terminal velocity proportional to the radius
Takes terminal velocity proportional to the cube of the radius (the volume)
Assumes all spheres of one material fall at the same terminal speed

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: A flat plate of area \( 0.1 \) m\(^2\) is pulled at 0.5 m/s over a horizontal surface on a film of oil 1 mm thick. The viscosity of the oil is 0.2 Pa s. The force needed is
questions.explanation:
Newton's law of viscosity: \( F=\eta A\dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta x} \).

Velocity gradient \( =\dfrac{0.5}{10^{-3}}=500 \) s\(^{-1}\).

\( F=0.2\times0.1\times500=10 \) N.
questions.hint: Velocity gradient = speed divided by film thickness (in metres).
distractor_logic: Forgets to convert the film thickness from millimetres to metres, making the gradient 1000 times too small
Slips a factor of ten in the velocity gradient
Uses the speed instead of the velocity gradient (speed divided by thickness)

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: Water (density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\), viscosity \( \eta=10^{-3} \) Pa s) flows at 0.02 m/s through a pipe of diameter 5 cm. The Reynolds number of the flow is
questions.explanation:
\( Re=\dfrac{\rho vd}{\eta}=\dfrac{1000\times0.02\times0.05}{10^{-3}} \).

Numerator \( =1 \), so \( Re=1000 \). The flow is at the upper edge of the laminar range.
questions.hint: Convert the diameter to metres before substituting.
distractor_logic: Forgets that the diameter is in centimetres and uses 0.005 m
Uses the diameter in centimetres without converting
Drops two powers of ten in the calculation

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: The dimensional formula of the coefficient of viscosity \( \eta \) is
questions.explanation:
\( \eta=\dfrac{F}{A}\cdot\dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta v} \).

\( [F/A]=[ML^{-1}T^{-2}] \) and \( [\Delta x/\Delta v]=[T] \).

Product: \( [ML^{-1}T^{-1}] \).
questions.hint: Multiply the dimensions of stress by the dimensions of time.
distractor_logic: This is the dimensional formula of momentum
This is the dimensional formula of pressure or stress, missing the time factor from the velocity gradient
This is the dimensional formula of surface tension

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: Large raindrops reach the ground faster than fine drizzle because
options: larger drops experience no air resistance
larger drops start falling from a greater height
terminal velocity increases with the square of the drop radius
gravity acts more strongly on larger drops per unit mass
questions.explanation:
From \( v_t=\dfrac{2r^2(\rho_{body}-\rho_{fluid})g}{9\eta} \), a drop with twice the radius has four times the terminal velocity.

Tiny drizzle drops therefore drift down slowly, while big raindrops fall fast.
questions.hint: Look at how \( r \) enters the terminal-velocity formula.
distractor_logic: All drops experience viscous drag; large drops simply need a higher speed for drag to balance weight
The starting height has nothing to do with the terminal speed
Gravitational acceleration is the same for all masses

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: An air bubble of radius \( r \) rises through water. Its steady speed of rise is given by the terminal-velocity formula with the density factor
options: \( \rho_{water} \) alone, with the bubble moving downward
questions.explanation:
Net force on the bubble = buoyancy minus weight \( =\tfrac43\pi r^3(\rho_{water}-\rho_{air})g \), directed upward.

At terminal velocity this is balanced by the downward Stokes drag \( 6\pi\eta rv_t \), so \( v_t=\dfrac{2r^2(\rho_{water}-\rho_{air})g}{9\eta} \), upward.
questions.hint: Which is larger for a bubble: weight or buoyancy?
distractor_logic: Ignores buoyancy entirely; for a bubble buoyancy is the dominant force
Buoyancy exceeds weight for a bubble, so the motion is upward, not downward
Gets the sign of the density difference backward; the net force is upward

questions.topic: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
questions.question: A soap bubble has radius 2 cm and the soap solution has surface tension \( T=0.03 \) N/m. The excess pressure inside the bubble is
questions.explanation:
A soap bubble has two surfaces, so \( P_{excess}=\dfrac{4T}{r} \).

\( P_{excess}=\dfrac{4\times0.03}{0.02}=6 \) Pa.
questions.hint: Bubble: four-T-over-r.
distractor_logic: Uses \( 2T/r \), the single-surface formula for a drop, forgetting the bubble's second surface
Uses \( 8T/r \), doubling once too often
Slips a factor of ten in the unit conversion

questions.topic: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
questions.question: A capillary tube of radius 0.5 mm is dipped in water (surface tension \( 0.07 \) N/m, density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\), angle of contact \( 0^\circ \)). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the height to which water rises is
questions.explanation:
\( h=\dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{\rho gr} \) with \( \cos0^\circ=1 \).

\( h=\dfrac{2\times0.07}{1000\times10\times5\times10^{-4}}=\dfrac{0.14}{5}=0.028 \) m \( =2.8 \) cm.
questions.hint: Two-T over rho-g-r, with the radius in metres.
distractor_logic: Uses \( T \) instead of \( 2T \) in the numerator
Uses the diameter in place of the radius, doubling the answer
Slips a factor of ten converting the radius to metres

questions.topic: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
questions.question: The work done in blowing a soap bubble of radius 5 cm from a solution of surface tension \( 0.03 \) N/m is
questions.explanation:
A bubble has two surfaces, so the total surface area is \( 2\times4\pi R^2=8\pi R^2 \).

Work \( =T\times8\pi R^2=0.03\times8\pi\times(0.05)^2=0.03\times8\pi\times0.0025=6\pi\times10^{-4} \) J.
questions.hint: Total area created = two surfaces of a sphere.
distractor_logic: Counts only one surface; a soap bubble has an inner and an outer surface
Doubles the surface count once too often
Uses \( 4\pi R^2T \) with an arithmetic slip in the radius squared

questions.topic: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
questions.question: A straight wire of length 10 cm is pulled out of a soap film of surface tension \( 0.03 \) N/m. The force due to surface tension on the wire is
questions.explanation:
The soap film has two free surfaces, each pulling on the wire with force \( Tl \).

Total force \( =2Tl=2\times0.03\times0.1=6\times10^{-3} \) N.
questions.hint: A film has two surfaces, so the effective length is doubled.
distractor_logic: Counts only one side of the film; the film has two surfaces touching the wire
Forgets to convert centimetres to metres
Uses one surface and forgets the unit conversion

questions.topic: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
questions.question: If the radius of a capillary tube is doubled, the height to which a liquid rises in it
questions.explanation:
\( h=\dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{\rho gr} \), so \( h\propto\dfrac{1}{r} \).

Doubling \( r \) halves \( h \).
questions.hint: Capillary rise is inversely proportional to the radius.
distractor_logic: Inverts the relationship; a wider tube supports a shorter column
Uses an inverse-square dependence; the rise varies as the inverse first power of the radius
Capillary rise clearly depends on tube radius

questions.topic: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
questions.question: Adding detergent to water helps it clean clothes better mainly because the detergent
options: increases the surface tension of water
lowers the surface tension of water, so it spreads into and wets the fabric fibres
makes the water denser so it sinks into the fabric
questions.explanation:
Detergent molecules collect at the water surface and reduce its surface tension.

Lower surface tension reduces the angle of contact with the fabric, so the water spreads and penetrates between the fibres, carrying dirt away.
questions.hint: Wetting improves when surface tension falls.
distractor_logic: Higher surface tension would make water bead up and wet fabric less
Density change is negligible; wetting is governed by surface tension and contact angle
Viscosity does not control wetting

questions.topic: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
questions.question: Two soap bubbles of different sizes are connected by a tube with a closed tap. When the tap is opened,
options: the larger bubble shrinks and the smaller bubble grows
both bubbles become equal in size
the smaller bubble shrinks and the larger bubble grows
nothing happens because both are at atmospheric pressure
questions.explanation:
Excess pressure inside a bubble is \( \dfrac{4T}{r} \), so the smaller bubble has the higher internal pressure.

When connected, air flows from the smaller (higher pressure) bubble to the larger (lower pressure) one.

The smaller bubble shrinks further and the larger grows.
questions.hint: Smaller radius, larger excess pressure.
distractor_logic: Air flows from higher to lower pressure, and the smaller bubble has the higher pressure
Equal size is not the equilibrium; air keeps flowing until the small one collapses
The pressure inside a bubble exceeds atmospheric by \( 4T/r \), and this differs for the two bubbles

questions.topic: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
questions.question: A capillary tube is shorter than the height to which the liquid would rise in it. When dipped in the liquid,
options: the liquid overflows from the top like a fountain
the liquid does not rise at all
the liquid rises to the calculated height by extending above the tube
the liquid rises to the top and the meniscus flattens, but it does not overflow
questions.explanation:
The rise is driven by the pressure drop across the curved meniscus, \( \dfrac{2T}{R} \), where \( R \) is the radius of curvature of the meniscus.

When the liquid reaches the top of the short tube, the meniscus becomes less curved (larger \( R \)) so that the reduced pressure difference just supports the shorter column.

No liquid overflows; energy conservation forbids a continuous fountain.
questions.hint: The meniscus can change its curvature.
distractor_logic: Overflow would be a perpetual-motion machine; the meniscus adjusts its curvature instead
The liquid still rises, up to the top of the tube
The liquid cannot rise beyond the physical top of the tube

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: A conical vessel (apex up, wide base down) and a cylindrical vessel have the same base area and are filled with a liquid to the same height. The liquid in the conical vessel weighs \( W \). The force exerted by the liquid on the base of the conical vessel is
questions.explanation:
The base force equals (pressure at the base) times (base area) \( =h\rho gA \), the same as for the cylinder of the same base and height.

The cylinder's liquid weighs \( h\rho gA \). A cone has one-third the volume of that cylinder, so the cone's liquid weighs \( W=\dfrac{h\rho gA}{3} \).

Hence the base force is \( h\rho gA=3W \). The extra \( 2W \) comes from the downward push of the inclined walls on the liquid.
questions.hint: Compare the cone with a cylinder of the same base and height: their base forces are equal.
distractor_logic: Assumes the base force equals the weight of the liquid; the walls of the cone also push down on the liquid
Inverts the volume ratio between cone and cylinder
Uses an incorrect cone-to-cylinder volume ratio of 1:2 instead of 1:3

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
