questions.question: A car of mass 1200 kg rests on the large piston of a hydraulic lift, whose area is \( 0.3 \) m\(^2\). The small piston has area \( 0.01 \) m\(^2\). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the minimum force on the small piston needed to support the car is
questions.explanation:
Weight of the car \( =1200\times10=12000 \) N.

Pressure is equal on both pistons: \( \dfrac{F}{0.01}=\dfrac{12000}{0.3} \).

\( F=12000\times\dfrac{0.01}{0.3}=400 \) N.
questions.hint: Equal pressure: force divided by area is the same on both pistons.
distractor_logic: Multiplies by the area ratio instead of dividing
Uses the mass in kilograms as if it were the required force
Slips a factor of ten in the area ratio

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: In a U-tube, water (density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\)) is on one side and a 10 cm column of oil (density \( 800 \) kg/m\(^3\)) is poured on the other side above the interface. The height of the water column above the interface level that balances the oil is
questions.explanation:
At the level of the oil-water interface the pressures on both arms must be equal.

\( h_{w}\rho_{w}g=h_{oil}\rho_{oil}g \), so \( h_{w}=10\times\dfrac{800}{1000}=8 \) cm.

The lighter oil needs a taller column, so the water column is shorter.
questions.hint: Equate pressures at the common horizontal level of the interface.
distractor_logic: Assumes equal heights balance, ignoring the density difference
Divides by the density ratio instead of multiplying
Applies the ratio 0.8 twice

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: A tank of water accelerates horizontally with acceleration \( a=5 \) m/s\(^2\). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the free surface of the water tilts so that \( \tan\theta \), where \( \theta \) is the angle the surface makes with the horizontal, equals
questions.explanation:
In the accelerating frame the water experiences an effective gravity with a horizontal component \( a \) (backward) and a vertical component \( g \).

The free surface sets itself perpendicular to this effective gravity, so \( \tan\theta=\dfrac{a}{g} \).

\( \tan\theta=\dfrac{5}{10}=0.5 \).
questions.hint: The free surface is always perpendicular to the effective gravity.
distractor_logic: Inverts the ratio, using \( g/a \) instead of \( a/g \)
Assumes the surface tilts at \( 45^\circ \) regardless of the acceleration
Assumes the surface stays horizontal; it does so only when the tank is at rest or moves uniformly

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: A sealed vessel filled with water is dropped and falls freely. The gauge pressure at any point inside the water during free fall is
options: still \( h\rho g \) at depth \( h \)
equal to atmospheric pressure at every point
questions.explanation:
Hydrostatic pressure arises from the weight of the liquid above a point: \( P_{gauge}=h\rho g_{eff} \).

During free fall the effective gravity is \( g_{eff}=g-g=0 \), so the water is weightless and no layer presses on the layer below.

The gauge pressure is therefore zero everywhere inside the water.
questions.hint: What is the effective gravity inside a freely falling frame?
distractor_logic: Uses the ordinary hydrostatic formula, but in free fall the effective gravity is zero so there is no hydrostatic pressure
No mechanism doubles the pressure; the water is weightless during free fall
Confuses gauge with absolute pressure; gauge pressure is measured relative to atmospheric pressure

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: A cube of side 20 cm is held fully submerged in water (density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\)) with its top face 30 cm below the surface and its faces horizontal and vertical. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the net force due to water pressure on the cube is
questions.explanation:
Forces on the vertical faces cancel in pairs. The net force comes from the difference in pressure between the bottom and top faces.

Pressure difference \( =\rho g\times(\text{height of cube})=1000\times10\times0.2=2000 \) Pa.

Face area \( =0.2\times0.2=0.04 \) m\(^2\), so net force \( =2000\times0.04=80 \) N upward. This is exactly the buoyant force.
questions.hint: Only the top and bottom faces contribute; find their pressure difference.
distractor_logic: Uses the depth of the top face (30 cm) instead of the height of the cube (20 cm) for the pressure difference
Uses the full depth of the bottom face (50 cm) instead of the difference between the two faces
Forgets to multiply the pressure difference by the face area

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: A block floats in water (density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\)) with three-quarters of its volume submerged. When it is placed in a liquid of density \( 1200 \) kg/m\(^3\), the fraction submerged becomes
questions.explanation:
From the water case, \( \dfrac{\rho_{block}}{1000}=\dfrac{3}{4} \), so \( \rho_{block}=750 \) kg/m\(^3\).

In the new liquid, fraction submerged \( =\dfrac{750}{1200}=\dfrac{5}{8} \).

A denser liquid supports the block with less of it under the surface.
questions.hint: First extract the block's density from the water case.
distractor_logic: Assumes the submerged fraction does not change with the liquid; a denser liquid needs less displaced volume
Multiplies the fraction by 1.2 instead of dividing by it; a denser liquid makes the block float higher
Uses an incorrect block density of 720 kg/m\(^3\)

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: A cube of side 10 cm and density \( 500 \) kg/m\(^3\) is pushed fully under water (density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\)). With \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the additional downward force needed to keep it fully submerged is
questions.explanation:
Volume \( =0.1^3=0.001 \) m\(^3\).

Buoyant force (fully submerged) \( =1000\times0.001\times10=10 \) N. Weight \( =500\times0.001\times10=5 \) N.

Extra downward force \( =10-5=5 \) N.
questions.hint: Full-submersion upthrust minus the cube's weight.
distractor_logic: Gives the full buoyant force; the cube's own weight already provides part of the balance
Adds the weight to the buoyancy instead of subtracting
Halves the correct value by using half the cube's volume

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: A wooden block of mass 300 g floats in water (density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\)) with three-quarters of its volume submerged. The mass that must be placed on top of the block (without touching the water) so that the block just becomes fully submerged is
questions.explanation:
Fraction submerged \( =\dfrac{\rho_{block}}{\rho_{water}}=\dfrac{3}{4} \), so \( \rho_{block}=750 \) kg/m\(^3\) and \( V=\dfrac{0.3}{750}=4\times10^{-4} \) m\(^3\).

Fully submerged, the block displaces \( 4\times10^{-4} \) m\(^3\) of water, of mass 400 g, so it can support a total of 400 g.

Added mass \( =400-300=100 \) g.
questions.hint: How much extra water does the last quarter of the volume displace?
distractor_logic: Assumes the added mass must equal the block's own mass
Takes one-quarter of the block's mass rather than the water displaced by the remaining quarter of the volume
Reports the total mass that the fully submerged block can support, not the added mass

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: A balloon of volume \( 100 \) m\(^3\) is filled with helium (density \( 0.16 \) kg/m\(^3\)) and released in air (density \( 1.2 \) kg/m\(^3\)). Ignoring the mass of the envelope and taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the net upward lifting force is
questions.explanation:
Buoyant force \( =\rho_{air}Vg=1.2\times100\times10=1200 \) N.

Weight of helium \( =0.16\times100\times10=160 \) N.

Net lift \( =1200-160=1040 \) N.
questions.hint: Lift = upthrust from air minus weight of the gas inside.
distractor_logic: Gives the buoyant force alone, forgetting to subtract the weight of the helium
Gives only the weight of the helium
Adds the helium weight to the buoyancy instead of subtracting

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: A beaker of water rests on a weighing scale. A person dips a finger into the water without touching the beaker. The scale reading
options: does not change, since the finger is not touching the beaker
decreases, since the finger supports part of the water
increases by an amount equal to the buoyant force on the finger
increases by the full weight of the finger
questions.explanation:
The water exerts an upward buoyant force \( F_B \) on the finger.

By Newton's third law, the finger exerts an equal downward force \( F_B \) on the water, which is transmitted to the beaker and the scale.

So the reading rises by exactly \( F_B \), the weight of the water displaced by the finger.
questions.hint: Action and reaction: if water pushes the finger up, what does the finger do to the water?
distractor_logic: Newton's third law: the water pushes up on the finger, so the finger pushes down on the water by an equal amount
The finger does not support the water; it displaces water and is pushed up by it
The finger is not resting on the water; only the buoyant force, not the finger's whole weight, is transmitted

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: A piece of ice with a small iron nail frozen inside floats in a glass of water. When the ice melts completely, the water level in the glass
options: rises if the nail is heavy enough
questions.explanation:
While floating, the ice-plus-nail displaces water equal to their combined weight. The nail, being denser than water, thereby displaces a volume of water larger than its own volume.

Melted ice turns into water of exactly the volume it displaced while floating, so that part causes no change.

The nail sinks and now displaces only its own volume, which is smaller. The water level falls.
questions.hint: Separate the ice's contribution from the nail's contribution.
distractor_logic: The nail, once sunk, displaces less water than it did while supported by the floating ice
The level stays the same only for pure ice; the dense nail changes the outcome
A heavier nail makes the level fall by more, not rise

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: Water (density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\)) enters a building's pipe at ground level at a gauge pressure of \( 2.0\times10^{5} \) Pa with speed 2 m/s. The pipe rises 5 m and narrows so that the speed becomes 4 m/s. With \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the gauge pressure at the upper point is
questions.hint: Both the rise and the speed-up lower the pressure.
distractor_logic: Includes the height drop but ignores the change in speed
Includes the speed change but ignores the 5 m rise
Adds the height and kinetic terms instead of subtracting them from the inlet pressure

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: In a horizontal venturi tube the inlet area is 3 times the throat area. A vertical tube attached at the inlet shows the water standing 40 cm higher than in a vertical tube at the throat. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the speed of water at the inlet is
questions.explanation:
Pressure difference \( P_1-P_2=\rho gh=1000\times10\times0.4=4000 \) Pa.

Continuity: \( v_2=3v_1 \). Bernoulli (horizontal): \( P_1-P_2=\tfrac12\rho(v_2^2-v_1^2)=\tfrac12\rho\cdot8v_1^2 \).

\( 4000=4000\,v_1^2 \), so \( v_1=1 \) m/s (and the throat speed is 3 m/s).
questions.hint: Use the manometer height for the pressure drop, continuity for the speed ratio, then Bernoulli.
distractor_logic: Reports the throat speed instead of the inlet speed
Forgets to divide \( 2gh \) by the factor \( (A_1/A_2)^2-1 \)
Forgets the square root as well as the area factor

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: A tank on level ground is filled with water to a height of 4 m. A small hole is made in its side 2 m below the water surface. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the horizontal distance from the tank at which the jet strikes the ground is
questions.explanation:
Speed of efflux: \( v=\sqrt{2gh}=\sqrt{2\times10\times2}=\sqrt{40} \) m/s.

The hole is \( 4-2=2 \) m above the ground, so the fall time is \( t=\sqrt{\dfrac{2\times2}{10}}=\sqrt{0.4} \) s.

Range \( =vt=\sqrt{40\times0.4}=\sqrt{16}=4 \) m. In general \( R=2\sqrt{h(H-h)} \).
questions.hint: Torricelli for the horizontal speed, then treat the jet as a projectile.
distractor_logic: Uses only the depth below the surface, not the projectile motion of the jet
Forgets that the hole is 2 m above the ground and uses the full 4 m as the fall height
Uses \( v\times t \) with the wrong time, doubling the range

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: Air (density \( 1 \) kg/m\(^3\)) flows over the upper surface of a wing at 60 m/s and under the lower surface at 50 m/s. The wing area is \( 10 \) m\(^2\). The dynamic lift on the wing is
questions.explanation:
Pressure difference across the wing: \( \Delta P=\tfrac12\rho(v_{top}^2-v_{bottom}^2)=\tfrac12\times1\times(3600-2500)=550 \) Pa.

Lift \( =\Delta P\times A=550\times10=5500 \) N.
questions.hint: Bernoulli gives the pressure difference; multiply by the area.
distractor_logic: Uses \( \tfrac12\rho(v_1-v_2)^2 \), the square of the speed difference, instead of the difference of the squares
Uses the speed difference multiplied by the average speed incorrectly, dropping part of the term
Forgets the factor one-half

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: Water leaves a tap with speed 1 m/s through an opening of area 1 cm\(^2\) and falls freely. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the cross-sectional area of the stream 40 cm below the tap is
questions.explanation:
Speed after falling 0.4 m: \( v^2=1^2+2\times10\times0.4=9 \), so \( v=3 \) m/s.

Continuity along the stream: \( A_1v_1=A_2v_2 \), so \( A_2=\dfrac{1\times1}{3}=\dfrac{1}{3} \) cm\(^2\).

This is why a falling stream of water gets thinner.
questions.hint: Find the speed after the fall, then apply continuity.
distractor_logic: Assumes the stream keeps the same area; the falling water speeds up so the stream narrows
Inverts the continuity relation, widening the stream instead of narrowing it
Squares the speed ratio; continuity involves the first power of the speed

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: A liquid flows steadily through a horizontal tube. At a wide section (area \( A \)) its speed is \( v \); at a narrow section the area is \( \dfrac{A}{2} \). Open vertical tubes are fitted at both sections. The difference in liquid heights in the two vertical tubes is
questions.explanation:
Continuity: speed at the narrow section \( =2v \).

Bernoulli (horizontal): \( P_1-P_2=\tfrac12\rho\left((2v)^2-v^2\right)=\tfrac32\rho v^2 \).

The vertical tubes show this pressure difference as a height difference \( \Delta h \) with \( \rho g\Delta h=\tfrac32\rho v^2 \), so \( \Delta h=\dfrac{3v^2}{2g} \). The liquid stands higher over the wide section.
questions.hint: Pressure difference from Bernoulli, then convert to a height using \( \rho g\Delta h \).
distractor_logic: Uses only the wide-section speed in the kinetic term, forgetting the narrow-section speed \( 2v \)
Uses the speed difference \( 2v-v=v \) squared instead of the difference of squares
Uses \( (2v)^2 \) alone, forgetting to subtract \( v^2 \)

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: A sphere of density \( 9000 \) kg/m\(^3\) is dropped first into liquid A (density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\), viscosity 1 Pa s) and then into liquid B (density \( 5000 \) kg/m\(^3\), viscosity 2 Pa s). The ratio of its terminal velocity in A to that in B is
questions.explanation:
\( v_t\propto\dfrac{\rho_{body}-\rho_{fluid}}{\eta} \) for the same sphere.

In A: \( \dfrac{9000-1000}{1}=8000 \). In B: \( \dfrac{9000-5000}{2}=2000 \).

Ratio \( =\dfrac{8000}{2000}=4 \).
questions.hint: Both the density difference and the viscosity change.
distractor_logic: Uses the sphere's density alone (ignoring buoyancy), which leaves only the viscosity ratio
Inverts the ratio
Uses the ratio of the sphere's density to the liquid densities incorrectly

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: Eight identical small drops, each falling with terminal velocity \( v \), coalesce into a single larger drop. The terminal velocity of the larger drop is
questions.explanation:
Volume is conserved: \( 8\times\tfrac43\pi r^3=\tfrac43\pi R^3 \), so \( R=2r \).

\( v_t\propto r^2 \), so the new terminal velocity is \( 2^2v=4v \).
questions.hint: Find the new radius from volume conservation, then use \( v_t\propto r^2 \).
distractor_logic: Assumes terminal velocity scales with volume (mass)
Assumes terminal velocity scales with the radius, which doubles
Assumes terminal velocity is independent of size

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: Two tubes of the same radius but lengths \( l \) and \( 2l \) are joined end to end, and a liquid flows steadily through the combination. The ratio of the pressure drop across the shorter tube to that across the longer tube is
questions.explanation:
In series the same volume flow rate \( Q \) passes through both tubes.

Poiseuille: \( Q=\dfrac{\pi\Delta Pr^4}{8\eta l} \), so for fixed \( Q \), \( r \) and \( \eta \), \( \Delta P\propto l \).

Ratio of pressure drops \( =\dfrac{l}{2l}=\dfrac12 \).
questions.hint: Same flow through both, so pressure drop is proportional to length.
distractor_logic: Inverts the ratio; a longer tube needs a larger pressure difference for the same flow
Assumes the pressure drop is independent of length
Uses the square of the length ratio

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: A sphere of density \( 2000 \) kg/m\(^3\) is released from rest in a liquid of density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\). Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), its acceleration at the instant its speed is half the terminal velocity is
questions.explanation:
Net downward force \( =(W-F_B)-F_{drag} \). With \( \rho_{fluid}=\tfrac12\rho_{body} \), buoyancy is half the weight, so \( W-F_B=\tfrac12mg \) and the initial acceleration is \( 5 \) m/s\(^2\).

Drag is proportional to speed and equals \( W-F_B \) at terminal velocity, so at half the terminal velocity the drag is \( \tfrac12(W-F_B) \).

Net force \( =\tfrac12(W-F_B)=\tfrac14mg \), giving \( a=2.5 \) m/s\(^2\).
questions.hint: Drag is linear in speed, so at half terminal speed it is half the net driving force.
distractor_logic: Gives the initial acceleration (just after release, before any drag acts)
Ignores both buoyancy and drag
Zero acceleration occurs only once the terminal velocity is fully reached

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: A steel ball of weight \( W \) falls through oil at its terminal velocity \( v \). Buoyancy is negligible. The rate at which mechanical energy is being converted into heat is
options: zero, since the ball moves at constant speed
questions.explanation:
At terminal velocity the viscous drag equals the weight \( W \) (buoyancy neglected).

Gravity does work at the rate \( Wv \), and since the kinetic energy is constant, all of it is dissipated by the drag.

Rate of heat production \( =F_{drag}\times v=Wv \).
questions.hint: Power = force times velocity; where does the work done by gravity go?
distractor_logic: No factor of one-half appears; power is force times velocity
Confuses power with kinetic energy
Constant speed means no change in kinetic energy, but gravity is still doing work that is dissipated as heat

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: Oil flows through a narrow tube under a fixed pressure difference. The oil is then warmed so that its viscosity halves, and at the same time it is passed through a tube of half the radius and the same length. The new volume flow rate is
questions.explanation:
\( Q\propto\dfrac{r^4}{\eta} \).

Halving \( r \): factor \( \dfrac{1}{16} \). Halving \( \eta \): factor \( 2 \).

Net factor \( =\dfrac{2}{16}=\dfrac18 \).
questions.hint: Radius to the fourth power in the numerator, viscosity in the denominator.
distractor_logic: Accounts for the radius but forgets that lower viscosity doubles the flow
Uses the square of the radius instead of the fourth power
Accounts only for the viscosity change and treats it as halving, ignoring the radius entirely

questions.topic: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
questions.question: A spherical water drop of radius 1 mm is broken into 8 identical smaller droplets. With surface tension \( T=0.07 \) N/m, the energy required is
options: zero, since the total volume is unchanged
questions.explanation:
Volume conservation: \( 8r^3=R^3 \), so \( r=\dfrac{R}{2}=0.5 \) mm.

Initial area \( =4\pi R^2 \). Final area \( =8\times4\pi r^2=8\times4\pi\dfrac{R^2}{4}=2\times4\pi R^2 \). Increase \( =4\pi R^2=4\pi\times10^{-6} \) m\(^2\).

Energy \( =T\times\Delta A=0.07\times4\pi\times10^{-6}=2.8\pi\times10^{-7} \) J.
questions.hint: Find the increase in total surface area, then multiply by \( T \).
distractor_logic: Uses the total final surface area instead of the increase in area
Slips a factor of ten in the radius conversion
Volume is conserved but the total surface area increases, which requires energy

questions.topic: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
questions.question: A capillary tube dipped in water shows a rise of 4 cm when at rest. It is then placed in a lift that accelerates upward with acceleration \( a=g \). The capillary rise becomes
questions.explanation:
\( h=\dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{\rho g_{eff}r} \), so \( h\propto\dfrac{1}{g_{eff}} \).

Upward acceleration \( a=g \) makes \( g_{eff}=2g \).

\( h_{new}=\dfrac{4}{2}=2 \) cm.
questions.hint: Replace \( g \) by the effective gravity in the lift.
distractor_logic: Inverts the effect; larger effective gravity means a shorter column
Assumes capillary rise is independent of gravity
The rise would become very large (not zero) only in free fall, where effective gravity vanishes

questions.topic: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
questions.question: A soap bubble of radius 1 cm is blown from a solution of surface tension \( 0.025 \) N/m. Atmospheric pressure is \( 1.0\times10^{5} \) Pa. The absolute pressure of the air inside the bubble is
questions.explanation:
Excess pressure inside a soap bubble \( =\dfrac{4T}{r}=\dfrac{4\times0.025}{0.01}=10 \) Pa.

Absolute pressure inside \( =P_{atm}+P_{excess}=1.0\times10^{5}+10 \) Pa.
questions.hint: Absolute inside pressure = atmospheric + excess.
distractor_logic: Uses the drop formula \( 2T/r \) for a two-surface bubble
Gives only the excess pressure, not the absolute pressure inside
Uses \( 8T/r \)

questions.topic: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
questions.question: A soap bubble of radius \( r \) is expanded isothermally to radius \( 2r \). If the surface tension of the solution is \( T \), the work done is
questions.explanation:
A bubble has two surfaces, so its total area is \( 8\pi R^2 \).

Increase in area \( =8\pi(2r)^2-8\pi r^2=8\pi r^2(4-1)=24\pi r^2 \).

Work \( =T\,\Delta A=24\pi r^2T \).
questions.hint: Two surfaces, and use the change in area.
distractor_logic: Counts only one surface of the bubble
Uses the final area alone rather than the increase in area
Uses the increase in area of a single sphere without the factor for two surfaces, and with the wrong radius

questions.topic: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
questions.question: A liquid rises to a height \( h \) in a capillary tube when its angle of contact with the tube is \( 0^\circ \). For a tube of the same radius made of a material with which the angle of contact is \( 60^\circ \), the rise would be
questions.explanation:
\( h=\dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{\rho gr} \), so \( h\propto\cos\theta \).

\( \cos60^\circ=\dfrac12 \) while \( \cos0^\circ=1 \).

New rise \( =\dfrac{h}{2} \).
questions.hint: The rise is proportional to the cosine of the contact angle.
distractor_logic: Assumes the rise is independent of the angle of contact
Uses \( \cos45^\circ \) instead of \( \cos60^\circ \)
Inverts the cosine factor

questions.topic: Surface Tension: Surface Energy, Excess Pressure, and Capillarity
questions.question: A liquid rises in a capillary tube. If the radius of the tube is doubled (same liquid, same material), the mass of liquid held in the raised column
questions.explanation:
Mass of the column \( =\rho\pi r^2h \), and \( h=\dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{\rho gr} \).

Substituting, mass \( =\dfrac{2\pi rT\cos\theta}{g} \), which is proportional to \( r \).

Doubling the radius doubles the mass of liquid lifted.
questions.hint: Combine the volume of the column with the capillary-rise formula.
distractor_logic: Only the height halves; the cross-section grows fourfold, so the net mass increases
Forgets that the height halves when the radius doubles
Mass changes because height and area scale differently with radius

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: A cube of side 10 cm is held fully submerged in water (density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\)) with its top face 20 cm below the surface. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the difference between the water pressure on the bottom face and on the top face, and the resulting buoyant force, are
questions.explanation:
Pressure difference between faces \( =\rho g\times\text{(side)}=1000\times10\times0.1=1000 \) Pa; the depth of the cube does not matter, only its height.

Buoyant force = pressure difference times face area \( =1000\times0.01=10 \) N.

This equals \( \rho_{water}Vg=1000\times0.001\times10=10 \) N, confirming Archimedes' principle arises from hydrostatic pressure.
questions.hint: Buoyancy is just the net effect of hydrostatic pressure on the faces.
distractor_logic: Uses the depth of the top face (20 cm) rather than the height of the cube (10 cm)
Uses the depth of the bottom face (30 cm)
Forgets to multiply by the face area correctly (uses 0.1 m\(^2\) instead of 0.01 m\(^2\))

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: A sphere is released in a liquid whose density is exactly equal to the sphere's density. The terminal-velocity formula \( v_t=\dfrac{2r^2(\rho_{body}-\rho_{fluid})g}{9\eta} \) predicts that the sphere
options: falls at a speed set by \( \rho_{body} \) alone
falls faster because there is no viscous drag
does not move: its weight is exactly balanced by buoyancy, so terminal velocity is zero
questions.explanation:
With \( \rho_{body}=\rho_{fluid} \), the buoyant force exactly equals the weight (Archimedes' principle).

The net driving force is zero, so no drag is needed to balance anything and the sphere stays wherever it is placed (neutral buoyancy).

The density difference in the formula is exactly what encodes this.
questions.hint: What is the net force when weight and buoyancy are equal?
distractor_logic: Ignores buoyancy, using the body density alone in the formula
Viscosity opposes motion; it cannot cause motion
Viscous drag is always present when there is motion; here there is no net driving force

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: A closed tank contains water (density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\)) with air above it at a gauge pressure of \( 3\times10^{4} \) Pa. A small hole is opened in the side of the tank 2 m below the water surface. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the speed of the emerging water is
questions.explanation:
Apply Bernoulli between the water surface (speed nearly zero, pressure \( P_{atm}+P_{gauge} \)) and the hole (pressure \( P_{atm} \), depth \( h \)).

\( \tfrac12\rho v^2=P_{gauge}+\rho gh \), so \( v^2=\dfrac{2P_{gauge}}{\rho}+2gh=\dfrac{2\times3\times10^{4}}{1000}+2\times10\times2=60+40=100 \).

\( v=10 \) m/s.
questions.hint: The extra air pressure acts like extra depth of water.
distractor_logic: Uses Torricelli's law with the depth alone, ignoring the extra air pressure
Uses the air pressure alone and ignores the 2 m depth
Forgets the square root after adding both contributions

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: Water (density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\)) rises 2 cm in a capillary tube. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the pressure just below the meniscus at the top of the column is
questions.explanation:
Inside the tube, the point level with the outside free surface is at atmospheric pressure (same horizontal level in a connected liquid at rest).

The top of the column is 2 cm above this point, so its pressure is lower by \( \rho gh=1000\times10\times0.02=200 \) Pa.

This deficit is exactly what the concave meniscus provides: \( \dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{r}=\rho gh \).
questions.hint: Go up 2 cm in a liquid at rest and the pressure drops by \( \rho gh \).
distractor_logic: Gets the sign wrong; a concave meniscus lowers the pressure beneath it, which is what lifts the column
Only the point at the level of the outside surface is at atmospheric pressure; the top of the column is 2 cm above it
Forgets to convert centimetres to metres

questions.question: A liquid flows through a horizontal pipe whose diameter halves at a certain point. The Reynolds number \( Re=\dfrac{\rho vd}{\eta} \) in the narrow part compared with the wide part is
questions.explanation:
Continuity: halving the diameter quarters the area, so the speed becomes \( 4v \).

\( Re\propto vd \): the speed factor is 4 and the diameter factor is \( \tfrac12 \).

Net factor \( =4\times\tfrac12=2 \). Narrowing a pipe pushes the flow toward turbulence.
questions.hint: Use continuity for the new speed, then substitute both changes.
distractor_logic: Both \( v \) and \( d \) change; they do not cancel
Correctly quadruples \( v \) but forgets that \( d \) is halved
Assumes a narrower pipe simply lowers the Reynolds number

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: A steel needle placed carefully on the surface of water floats, although steel is much denser than water. This is because
options: the needle displaces enough water for buoyancy to balance its weight
the needle has a lower density than water when dry
air trapped around the needle makes it lighter than water
surface tension of the water surface supports the needle, not buoyancy
questions.explanation:
A floating body is normally supported by buoyancy, which requires displacing water of weight equal to the body's weight. A dense steel needle would have to be almost entirely submerged for that, which would make it sink.

Instead, the needle rests in a small depression of the surface. The stretched surface pulls upward along the line of contact, and the vertical component of this surface-tension force balances the needle's weight.

Adding detergent lowers the surface tension and the needle sinks.
questions.hint: Compare the water displaced by a dent with the water displaced by a submerged needle.
distractor_logic: The needle barely dents the surface and displaces far too little water for buoyancy to balance its weight
Steel's density does not change with dryness
Trapped air is not the mechanism; the curved water surface exerts an upward force

questions.topic: Viscosity: Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Poiseuille's Equation
questions.question: Tiny water droplets in a mist are nearly perfect spheres and fall extremely slowly, while large raindrops fall fast. The two observations are explained, respectively, by
options: surface tension minimising the surface area, and terminal velocity being proportional to the square of the radius
viscosity of water making small drops round, and gravity being weaker on small drops
air pressure compressing small drops, and large drops having no air resistance
surface tension making small drops round, and terminal velocity being proportional to the radius
questions.explanation:
Surface tension makes a free drop take the shape of least surface area for its volume: a sphere. For small drops this dominates over any distortion by air flow.

From \( v_t=\dfrac{2r^2(\rho_{body}-\rho_{fluid})g}{9\eta} \), halving the radius quarters the terminal velocity, so mist droplets drift very slowly.
questions.hint: One fact from surface tension, one from Stokes' law.
distractor_logic: Viscosity does not set the shape, and gravity per unit mass is the same for all drops
Air pressure is uniform, and all drops feel air resistance
Correct shape mechanism but the terminal velocity depends on the square of the radius, not the first power

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: A hydrometer (a weighted float with a graduated stem) is placed first in water and then in a liquid less dense than water. In the lighter liquid the hydrometer
options: floats higher, because the lighter liquid exerts more upthrust
sinks deeper, because a larger displaced volume is needed to balance its weight
floats at the same level, because its weight is unchanged
sinks deeper, because the pressure at its base is greater
questions.explanation:
For a floating body, \( \rho_{fluid}V_{displaced}g= \) weight, so \( V_{displaced}\propto\dfrac{1}{\rho_{fluid}} \).

A less dense liquid requires a larger displaced volume, so the hydrometer sinks further.

This is why the density markings on a hydrometer stem increase downward.
questions.hint: Same weight to support, less dense liquid, more volume displaced.

Weight is unchanged, but the volume required to displace an equal weight of a lighter liquid is larger

questions.question: Water (density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\)) is siphoned out of a large open tank. The highest point of the siphon tube is 2 m above the water surface, and the outlet is 5 m below the water surface. Taking \( P_{atm}=1.0\times10^{5} \) Pa and \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), the absolute pressure at the highest point of the siphon is

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: A needle floats on water. A drop of detergent is added to the water far from the needle. Soon after, the needle sinks. The best explanation is
options: the surface tension falls, so the surface can no longer support the needle, while the buoyant force on it was always too small
the detergent increases the density of the needle
the detergent reduces the buoyant force on the needle
the detergent increases the viscosity of water
questions.explanation:
The needle was held up by surface tension, not by buoyancy (a steel needle displaces far too little water when resting on the surface).

Detergent lowers the surface tension, reducing the upward surface-tension force below the needle's weight.

The needle then breaks through the surface, and since it is denser than water, buoyancy cannot save it.
questions.hint: Which force was actually supporting the needle?
distractor_logic: Detergent cannot change the needle's density

questions.topic: Pressure in Fluids: Pascal's Law, Hydrostatic Pressure, and Pressure Measurement
questions.question: Water flows out of a wide tank through a long horizontal capillary tube attached near its bottom. A second, identical tube is now attached in parallel next to the first. With the water level held fixed, the total volume flow rate out of the tank
options: remains the same, because the pressure head is unchanged
increases sixteenfold, because the effective radius doubles
doubles, because each tube carries the same Poiseuille flow under the same pressure head
increases by a factor \( \sqrt{2} \), by Torricelli's law
questions.explanation:
With the level fixed, both tubes experience the same pressure difference \( \rho gh \) across the same length.

Poiseuille's equation gives each tube the same flow rate \( Q=\dfrac{\pi\rho ghr^4}{8\eta l} \).

Flows in parallel add, so the total is \( 2Q \).
questions.hint: Same head across each tube; flows in parallel add.
distractor_logic: Each tube independently carries the same flow, so two tubes carry twice as much
Two separate tubes of radius \( r \) are not equivalent to one tube of radius \( 2r \); flows simply add
Torricelli's law is for an ideal fluid leaving a hole, not for viscous flow through long tubes

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: Two spheres of the same radius, one of density \( 2000 \) kg/m\(^3\) and the other of density \( 3000 \) kg/m\(^3\), fall through water (density \( 1000 \) kg/m\(^3\)). The ratio of their terminal velocities (lighter to heavier) is
questions.explanation:
\( v_t\propto(\rho_{body}-\rho_{fluid}) \) for the same radius, fluid and viscosity.

Lighter: \( 2000-1000=1000 \). Heavier: \( 3000-1000=2000 \).

Ratio \( =1000:2000=1:2 \). Buoyancy makes the difference larger than the bare density ratio 2:3 would suggest.
questions.hint: Subtract the fluid's density from each before taking the ratio.
distractor_logic: Uses the ratio of the spheres' densities alone, ignoring the buoyancy of water
Assumes terminal velocity depends only on the radius
Inverts the ratio of body densities

questions.topic: Fluid Dynamics: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
questions.question: Water flows through a horizontal pipe that narrows from area \( A \) to \( \dfrac{A}{4} \). A student calculates the speed ratio using Bernoulli's equation and the pressure ratio using the equation of continuity. The correct approach is
options: speed ratio from continuity (it becomes 4 times), then pressure difference from Bernoulli (it falls in the narrow part)
speed ratio from Bernoulli and pressure ratio from continuity, as the student did
both from continuity, since mass is conserved
both from Bernoulli, since energy is conserved
questions.explanation:
The equation of continuity, \( A_1v_1=A_2v_2 \), is a statement of mass conservation and relates speed to cross-sectional area only: here \( v_2=4v_1 \).

Bernoulli's equation, \( P+\tfrac12\rho v^2=\text{constant} \) for a horizontal pipe, then converts the known speeds into a pressure difference: \( P_1-P_2=\tfrac12\rho(16v_1^2-v_1^2)=\tfrac{15}{2}\rho v_1^2 \).

The narrow section has higher speed and lower pressure.
questions.hint: Continuity for speeds, Bernoulli for pressures, in that order.
distractor_logic: Continuity links speed to area; Bernoulli links pressure to speed; the student has swapped them
Continuity says nothing about pressure
Bernoulli alone cannot give the speed ratio without knowing the pressures; continuity supplies the speeds first

questions.topic: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
questions.question: A ball bearing of radius \( r \) falls through oil and reaches terminal velocity \( v \). A second bearing of radius \( 2r \), made of the same steel, falls through the same oil. Compare the buoyant force and the terminal velocity of the second bearing with the first.
options: buoyant force 4 times, terminal velocity 4 times
buoyant force 8 times, terminal velocity 4 times
buoyant force 8 times, terminal velocity 8 times
buoyant force 2 times, terminal velocity 2 times
questions.explanation:
Buoyant force \( =\rho_{oil}\tfrac43\pi r^3g\propto r^3 \): doubling \( r \) gives 8 times.

Terminal velocity \( v_t=\dfrac{2r^2(\rho_{body}-\rho_{fluid})g}{9\eta}\propto r^2 \): doubling \( r \) gives 4 times.

The weight also grows 8 times, so the net driving force is 8 times but the drag coefficient \( 6\pi\eta r \) only doubles, leaving a fourfold speed.
questions.hint: Volume goes as the cube; terminal velocity as the square.
distractor_logic: Buoyancy scales with displaced volume, which goes as the cube of the radius, not the square
Terminal velocity goes as the square of the radius, not the cube
Both quantities depend on higher powers of the radius than the first
